## Learning Objective

Explain the assumptions of the Cox proportional hazards model.


## Lesson


The Cox proportional hazards model has the following assumptions,
where $h_i(t)$ is the hazard rate for the $i$th observation
and $h_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard rate:

1. $\log h_i(t) = \log h_0(t) + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$
2. The observations are iid.
3. Censoring is independent of time to event.

Note that there's no $\beta_0$.
With the Cox proportional hazards model (which I will abbreviate to
the Cox model or Cox regression),
we don't estimate an intercept.
This means we don't estimate the baseline hazard rate.
At no point do we say what $h_0(t)$ is.

We can write the first assumption above with exponents instead of logs:
$$
h_i(t) = h_0(t) \exp\left(\beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \text{.}
$$


## Problems

### Problem 1

Compare and contrast these assumptions with those of a generalized linear
model.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Similarities:

- We have a linear function of the covariates,
i.e., $\beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$.
- We're modeling the log of the hazard,
which is similar to modeling the log of the rate or mean in Poisson regression.
- We assume the observations are independent.

Differences:

- There's no $\beta_0$.
- We don't assume a distribution for the time to the event.
This implies there's no assumed mean-variance relationship.
- Here, we have to make an additional assumption about censoring.

:::
